Name: Talc
Fact 1: Mohs hardness reference mineral 1: the softest mineral
Fact 2: Ground into talcum powder
Fact 3: Main mineral of soapstone, a soft carving stone that feels soapy
Fact 4: Magnesium sheet silicate used as a filler in ceramics and paper

Name: Gypsum
Fact 1: Mohs hardness reference mineral 2: scratched by a fingernail
Fact 2: Used to make plaster and drywall
Fact 3: Selenite and desert rose are varieties of it
Fact 4: Hydrated calcium sulfate whose thick beds mark ancient evaporated seas
Fact 5: Most modern blackboard chalk is made of it

Name: Calcite
Fact 1: Mohs hardness reference mineral 3
Fact 2: The classic mineral that fizzes strongly in cold dilute acid
Fact 3: Clear crystals (Iceland spar) show double refraction, which was key to early optics
Fact 4: Main mineral of limestone and marble, among Earth's largest carbon stores
Fact 5: Heated to make lime and cement

Name: Fluorite
Fact 1: Mohs hardness reference mineral 4
Fact 2: Often forms purple or green cubes
Fact 3: Many samples glow under UV light, and the word "fluorescence" comes from it
Fact 4: The element fluorine is named after it
Fact 5: Main source of fluorine for hydrofluoric acid, Teflon and refrigerants
Fact 6: Calcium halide used as a flux in steelmaking (its name comes from Latin for "to flow")

Name: Apatite
Fact 1: Mohs hardness reference mineral 5
Fact 2: The mineral that makes up teeth and bones
Fact 3: Main source of phosphate fertilizer, which has no substitute in farming

Name: Orthoclase
Fact 1: Mohs hardness reference mineral 6
Fact 2: Pink potassium feldspar that gives granite its pink color
Fact 3: Monoclinic, higher-temperature form of potassium feldspar (KAlSi3O8)

Name: Quartz
Fact 1: Mohs hardness reference mineral 7: scratches glass
Fact 2: Amethyst, citrine and rose quartz are varieties of it
Fact 3: Second most common mineral in Earth's crust and the main grain in sand
Fact 4: Raw material for glass and silicon chips
Fact 5: Piezoelectric crystals of it keep time in watches and electronics

Name: Topaz
Fact 1: Mohs hardness reference mineral 8
Fact 2: Gemstone that is colorless when pure, often blue (usually from treatment) or golden
Fact 3: Fluorine-bearing aluminum silicate gem that marks fluorine-rich granites and pegmatites, often with tin and tungsten

Name: Corundum
Fact 1: Mohs hardness reference mineral 9
Fact 2: Its red gem variety is ruby
Fact 3: Every gem color of it except red is called sapphire
Fact 4: Aluminum oxide used as an abrasive (emery)
Fact 5: Grown synthetically as "sapphire glass" for watch faces and phone camera covers
Fact 6: The first laser (1960) used a crystal of its red variety

Name: Diamond
Fact 1: Mohs hardness reference mineral 10: the hardest natural mineral
Fact 2: Carbon mineral that forms deep in the mantle; same element as graphite in a different structure
Fact 3: Best natural conductor of heat
Fact 4: The hardest material, used to tip cutting and drilling tools
Fact 5: Its crystals and their inclusions are samples brought up from the deep mantle

Name: Graphite
Fact 1: Same element as diamond, but in sheets that slide over each other, so it is very soft
Fact 2: Pencil "lead"
Fact 3: The anode in every lithium-ion battery
Fact 4: Carbon mineral used as a dry lubricant and for steelmaking electrodes
Fact 5: A single layer of it is graphene

Name: Gold
Fact 1: Very dense, soft native metal that never tarnishes
Fact 2: The native metal that has stored monetary value through human history
Fact 3: Plated onto electronic contacts because it never corrodes

Name: Silver
Fact 1: Native metal that often forms wiry growths
Fact 2: Native metal that tarnishes black
Fact 3: The best electrical and heat conductor of all metals
Fact 4: Native metal used for coins, film photography, and now solar panels

Name: Copper
Fact 1: Native metal that tarnishes brown to green, often in branching (dendritic) masses
Fact 2: Probably the first metal humans worked
Fact 3: The metal that carries electricity in nearly all wiring

Name: Sulfur
Fact 1: Bright yellow native element that forms around volcanic vents
Fact 2: Raw material for sulfuric acid, the most produced industrial chemical
Fact 3: Yellow native element used in gunpowder and to vulcanize rubber

Name: Pyrite
Fact 1: "Fool's gold": brassy cubes, harder and more brittle than gold
Fact 2: The most common sulfide mineral
Fact 3: Iron sulfide whose weathering causes acid mine drainage
Fact 4: Cubic iron sulfide once roasted to make sulfuric acid

Name: Marcasite
Fact 1: Same formula as pyrite in a different (orthorhombic) structure; paler
Fact 2: Iron sulfide that crumbles over time ("pyrite decay"), damaging museum specimens

Name: Galena
Fact 1: Main ore of lead
Fact 2: Heavy, silvery cubes that break into smaller cubes
Fact 3: Lead sulfide that is also a major source of silver
Fact 4: Early crystal radios used it as the detector ("cat's whisker")

Name: Sphalerite
Fact 1: Main ore of zinc
Fact 2: Zinc sulfide, usually brown to black with a resinous shine
Fact 3: Byproduct source of germanium, gallium and indium for electronics

Name: Chalcopyrite
Fact 1: The world's most important copper ore
Fact 2: Brassy yellow copper-iron sulfide, often with an iridescent tarnish

Name: Cinnabar
Fact 1: Main ore of mercury
Fact 2: Bright red, toxic mercury sulfide
Fact 3: Ground to make vermilion, a red pigment used since ancient times

Name: Molybdenite
Fact 1: Soft, silvery flakes that look like graphite but are a sulfide
Fact 2: Main ore of molybdenum, which strengthens steel
Fact 3: Sulfide whose rhenium content allows rhenium-osmium (Re-Os) dating
Fact 4: A single layer of it is a 2D semiconductor, a counterpart to graphene

Name: Stibnite
Fact 1: Long, metallic, needle-like crystals of a sulfide
Fact 2: Main ore of antimony, a critical mineral used in flame retardants, batteries and ammunition
Fact 3: Ground to make the ancient eyeliner kohl

Name: Halite
Fact 1: Rock salt: tastes salty and forms cubes
Fact 2: Spread on roads to melt ice
Fact 3: Starting point of the chlorine and lye (chlor-alkali) industry
Fact 4: Forms underground domes that trap oil and are used to store fuel and waste

Name: Sylvite
Fact 1: Looks like halite but tastes more bitter
Fact 2: Major source of potash, supplying the K in N-P-K fertilizer

Name: Hematite
Fact 1: Main ore of iron, and so the basis of steel
Fact 2: Can look black and metallic, but always leaves a red-brown streak
Fact 3: Iron oxide in banded iron formations that record the rise of oxygen in the atmosphere
Fact 4: Makes Mars and many red rocks red
Fact 5: Ground into red ochre, humanity's first pigment

Name: Magnetite
Fact 1: The most strongly magnetic natural mineral
Fact 2: Lodestone, which made the first compasses, is a naturally magnetized form of it
Fact 3: Iron oxide whose grains record past magnetic fields in rocks, key evidence for plate tectonics

Name: Ilmenite
Fact 1: Black, weakly magnetic main ore of titanium
Fact 2: Main source of titanium dioxide, the white pigment in paint, paper, plastics and sunscreen

Name: Chromite
Fact 1: The only ore of chromium
Fact 2: The ore of the metal that makes stainless steel stainless

Name: Spinel
Fact 1: Its red variety was long mistaken for ruby
Fact 2: The Black Prince's Ruby in the British crown is actually this mineral
Fact 3: Magnesium aluminum oxide that names a crystal structure found in the mantle and in battery cathodes

Name: Cassiterite
Fact 1: Main ore of tin; heavy and usually brown to black
Fact 2: The ore whose tin made bronze, and so the Bronze Age, possible
Fact 3: Tin oxide ore listed as a conflict mineral; its tin goes into electronics solder

Name: Goethite
Fact 1: Iron hydroxide that is a major part of rust
Fact 2: Main coloring mineral of yellow-brown ochre
Fact 3: Gives soils and tropical laterites their yellow-brown color
Fact 4: Iron hydroxide found on Mars as evidence of past water

Name: Aragonite
Fact 1: Same formula as calcite in a different (orthorhombic) structure
Fact 2: Makes up corals, pearls and many shells
Fact 3: The carbonate mineral at the center of concerns about ocean acidification

Name: Dolomite
Fact 1: Like calcite, but fizzes only weakly in acid unless powdered
Fact 2: Gives its name to a mountain range in the Italian Alps
Fact 3: Calcium magnesium carbonate whose rare formation today is a long-standing geological puzzle

Name: Siderite
Fact 1: Brown iron carbonate; an iron ore
Fact 2: Iron carbonate that forms only in low-oxygen conditions, a clue to early Earth and Mars

Name: Rhodochrosite
Fact 1: Pink to red carbonate, often banded
Fact 2: Manganese carbonate ore prized as a collector's and gem mineral

Name: Azurite
Fact 1: Deep blue copper carbonate, often found with malachite and slowly turning into it
Fact 2: Blue pigment of medieval and Renaissance paintings
Fact 3: Its blue stains on rock point prospectors to copper deposits

Name: Barite
Fact 1: Unusually heavy for a light-colored mineral; often bladed crystals
Fact 2: Mostly used to weight oil-well drilling mud
Fact 3: Barium sulfate given as a "barium meal" for X-ray imaging

Name: Anhydrite
Fact 1: Gypsum without the water; turns into gypsum when it absorbs water
Fact 2: Calcium sulfate that swells as it turns to gypsum, damaging tunnels and foundations

Name: Olivine
Fact 1: Olive-green mineral common in basalt
Fact 2: Main mineral of the upper mantle, probably the most abundant mineral in Earth's upper layers
Fact 3: Its gem form is peridot
Fact 4: Green magnesium-iron silicate that weathers quickly and is studied for capturing CO2

Name: Garnet
Fact 1: Red-brown mineral group common in metamorphic rocks; almandine is the common one
Fact 2: Mineral group petrologists use to work out the pressure and temperature a metamorphic rock went through
Fact 3: Mineral group used as an abrasive for waterjet cutting and sandpaper

Name: Zircon
Fact 1: Durable mineral that keeps its uranium-lead clock, so it is the main mineral for dating rocks
Fact 2: Grains of it over 4.4 billion years old are the oldest known pieces of Earth and show early Earth had water
Fact 3: Ore of zirconium, used in nuclear reactor fuel cladding

Name: Beryl
Fact 1: Its green variety is emerald
Fact 2: Its blue-green variety is aquamarine
Fact 3: Main ore of beryllium, used in aerospace alloys and X-ray windows

Name: Tourmaline
Fact 1: Long, striated prisms; the common variety (schorl) is black
Fact 2: Gem mineral group in many colors, including pink-and-green "watermelon" slices
Fact 3: Gem silicate that is pyroelectric and piezoelectric: heating or squeezing it builds up charge
Fact 4: The main mineral that holds boron in rocks

Name: Hornblende
Fact 1: The most common amphibole; dark, elongated crystals common in granite and diorite
Fact 2: Amphibole whose aluminum content is used to estimate the pressure at which igneous rocks crystallized

Name: Muscovite
Fact 1: Clear to silvery mica that peels into thin, flexible sheets
Fact 2: Mica used for stove windows ("isinglass") and electrical insulation
Fact 3: Light-colored mica whose potassium is used for argon-argon dating

Name: Kaolinite
Fact 1: White clay mineral used in porcelain ("china clay")
Fact 2: Clay mineral that forms when feldspar weathers
Fact 3: White clay that coats glossy paper and gave its name to the medicine Kaopectate

Name: Serpentine
Fact 1: Group of green minerals that form when olivine reacts with water
Fact 2: Its fibrous form (chrysotile) is a type of asbestos
Fact 3: Its formation at seafloor vents releases hydrogen and methane, possibly where life began
Fact 4: Hydrated mineral group that carries water down into subduction zones

Name: Microcline
Fact 1: Same formula as orthoclase, but triclinic
Fact 2: Its green variety is amazonite
Fact 3: Low-temperature potassium feldspar that often forms giant crystals in pegmatites
